title: Lockheed's PAC-3 Edge and a B-52 Anti-Ship Pitch Headline a Week of Interceptor and Missile Deals
subhead: Lockheed Martin unveiled a new Patriot interceptor aimed at hypersonic threats and the US Navy moved to arm the B-52 with anti-ship missiles, as Riyadh counted 12 dead from Houthi strikes on its main airport and NATO ran its largest command-post exercise of the year.

sections.heading: Lockheed unveils PAC-3 Edge as the interceptor market heats up
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin has unveiled a new Patriot interceptor called the PAC-3 Edge, pitched against emerging hypersonic threats, according to Breaking Defense and Defense News. The reveal comes days after Boeing locked in a 7-year deal, reported at roughly $14.7 billion by Army Technology, to triple PAC-3 MSE seeker output — a bottleneck that has constrained Patriot production for years.

The two moves point at the same problem: demand for air and missile defense interceptors is outrunning the industrial base. Lockheed is positioning a next-generation round while Boeing invests in the seeker supply chain that feeds current PAC-3s. Army Technology reported the Boeing contract on Oct 6; the Lockheed Edge reveal followed on Oct 9-10.
sections.whyItMatters: Interceptor production capacity — not budget — is the binding constraint on air defense in Europe, the Gulf and the Indo-Pacific. A new round plus a seeker expansion signals the US industrial base is being rebuilt around volume, not just capability.

sections.heading: US Navy to arm the B-52 with LRASM anti-ship missiles
sections.body:
The US Navy's Naval Air Systems Command plans to award Lockheed Martin a contract to integrate the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) onto the US Air Force's B-52 bomber, according to an Oct 7 notice reported by Air & Space Forces Magazine and relayed by Defence Industry Europe. The planned work covers missile software updates, testing, test-asset repair and failure review boards.

The B-52 can already carry up to 20 JASSM (Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles) — the weapon on which LRASM is based — and their similar dimensions raise the prospect of a comparable anti-ship load. Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger of the Mitchell Institute told the magazine that a handful of B-52s could deliver more weapons against maritime targets, over far longer ranges, than the Navy's carrier-based aircraft can per day. The plan follows a June disclosure that a B-2A Spirit used LRASM against a decommissioned amphibious transport during a Pacific exercise — the first US acknowledgment of the B-2 carrying the missile.
sections.whyItMatters: Distributing anti-ship strike across bombers turns a handful of aircraft into a long-range maritime-denial salvo — a capability aimed squarely at contested waters in the Pacific, and a signal that the US is widening the platforms it can launch standoff anti-ship weapons from.

sections.heading: Houthi strikes kill 12 at Riyadh's King Khalid airport; Washington weighs joining the fight
sections.body:
Attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people, including 4 Saudis and 8 foreigners, and suspended operations at the hub, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage and BBC News. Yemen's Houthis said they fired two ballistic missiles at the airport and also targeted Najran airport and Khamis Mushait air base; Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the latter two claims. The BBC reported one of the dead was a pilot of state carrier Saudia, whose aircraft was struck in a second attack.

The escalation drew a US response: President Trump condemned the 'terrible' attack and said the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis, per Al Jazeera and TASS. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attack on Riyadh airport, which he said killed an American (TASS). The strikes fit a pattern of Houthi drone-and-missile attacks on Saudi airports through early October — including Abha and Najran — that have killed civilians.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthis are now holding Saudi civilian aviation and air bases at risk with ballistic missiles and drones, forcing a decision point in Washington on direct intervention. It is also a live demonstration of how cheap missiles and one-way attack drones can shut a major hub — the central air-defense and counter-drone procurement problem of the moment.

sections.heading: NATO runs Steadfast Duel 2026, its largest command-post exercise
sections.body:
NATO's Steadfast Duel 2026 is underway with roughly 8,000 military and civilian personnel across Europe and the United States, Defence Industry Europe reported. It is the alliance's largest annual computer-assisted command-post exercise, training collective defense under Article 5 at the operational and higher tactical levels, focused on the northwest region.

SHAPE scheduled the exercise and the Joint Warfare Centre directs it, covering the Allied Command Operations warfighting system — SHAPE, three joint force commands, seven domain component commands and the Allied Reaction Force. All 32 allies support it, alongside NATO HQ, US European Command and partner organizations. Maj. Gen. Ruprecht von Butler, commander of the Joint Warfare Centre, said the exercise tests 'our defence plans, readiness' as a top priority.
sections.whyItMatters: A 32-member command-post drill is where new regional defense plans — and the logistics and C2 assumptions behind them — get stress-tested without firing a shot. It is the operational counterpart to the spending pledges that dominate the political headlines.

sections.heading: Baykar scores first Akinci firing test with Aselsan's Morfoz guidance kit
sections.body:
Turkey's Baykar reported a direct hit in the first firing test of its Akinci unmanned combat aircraft using Aselsan's Morfoz Guidance Kit (MGK), the company said, per Defence Industry Europe. The test took place over the Gulf of Saros as part of the aircraft's weapons integration program, with the drone flying from the Çorlu Flight Training and Test Center in Tekirdağ carrying the MGK alongside an Alpagut munition developed by Roketsan and STM.

Baykar said Aselsan developed the MGK entirely with Turkish components. It joins a broad set of indigenous munitions already integrated on the Akinci, including the MAM series, the TOLUN family, the TEBER, GÖKÇE and GÖZDE guidance kits, the İHA-300/230/122 supersonic missiles, the ÇAKIR cruise missile, the EREN loitering munition and the SUNGUR air-defense missile.
sections.whyItMatters: Each indigenous guidance-kit integration deepens Turkey's independence from foreign components and strengthens its export offer for armed drones — a market where Ankara is already a leading supplier, and where buyers increasingly want munitions decoupled from US or European supply chains.

sections.heading: Northrop launches 21 Link 16 satellites as missile-tracking constellation grows
sections.body: Northrop Grumman deployed 21 satellites for the Space Development Agency's Tranche 1 Transport Layer, forming the company's first orbital plane in a network designed to deliver secure tactical communications and carry missile-tracking data, Defence Industry Europe reported. The Transport Layer is part of SDA's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture, a low-Earth-orbit constellation built to detect and track missiles and move data rapidly worldwide, connecting military users with missile-tracking satellites on an interoperable network.
sections.whyItMatters: A space-based sensor and comms layer is the enabling infrastructure for missile warning and for hitting moving or time-sensitive targets — including the anti-ship and hypersonic-defense missions that the week's missile deals are designed for. Constellation build-out is now the pacing item for a lot of that capability.

sections.heading: Sustainment and exports round-up: Honeywell's F-35 test cell, Australia's HIMARS, Philippines Black Hawks
sections.body:
Honeywell Aerospace and Netherlands-based Aeronamic brought a modular test cell into operation at Woensdrecht Air Support Command, enabling regional testing of turbomachines used in the F-35's Power and Thermal Management System — a step toward establishing repair capability in Europe, per Defence Industry Europe.

Separately, Australia received its second HIMARS tranche two years ahead of schedule, Army Technology reported — a rare delivery acceleration in a period defined by backlog. Lockheed Martin was contracted to supply a Black Hawk simulator suite to the Philippines, and Romania ordered 12 Airbus H225M helicopters under the EU's SAFE framework, according to Airforce Technology. Boeing also secured the 7-year PAC-3 MSE seeker deal noted above, and Raytheon was reported by Naval Technology to have won a contract worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB missiles.
sections.whyItMatters: These sustainment, training and export contracts are where rearmament actually lands: European F-35 upkeep, Indo-Pacific helicopter and HIMARS deliveries, and a large naval interceptor buy. Delivery timelines and regional repair capacity now matter as much as the headline value of a deal.

bottomLine: Today's defense-industrial thread is capacity: Lockheed's new PAC-3 Edge and Boeing's 7-year seeker expansion both attack the interceptor bottleneck, while the US Navy moves to make the B-52 a long-range anti-ship shooter and Northrop pushes a 21-satellite missile-tracking plane into orbit. In the field, the week's most consequential event was the Houthi missile strikes that killed 12 at Riyadh's main airport, forcing Washington to weigh joining Saudi retaliation and showing how cheap missiles and drones can shut a major hub. NATO's 8,000-person Steadfast Duel and a wave of sustainment and export deals — Honeywell's European F-35 test cell, Australia's accelerated HIMARS, Romania's H225M buy — confirm that the alliance's operational and industrial build-out is proceeding alongside the political spending debate.
sources: Breaking Defense, Defense News, Army Technology, Naval Technology, Airforce Technology, Defence Industry Europe, Air & Space Forces Magazine, Al Jazeera, BBC News, TASS, Defense One
